title: The piece you picked is the faintest block on the strip
goal: Cut a recording into pieces and the piece you are holding, the one Delete takes, is drawn dimmer than the pieces you are not holding. A piece you have already played through is a solid mid grey block; the piece you just picked, before the playhead has moved into it, is a nearly empty dark box with a thin coloured outline round it. So the strongest thing on the strip says how far you have watched, and the faintest thing on it says what is about to be deleted. Make the picked piece the one that reads first.
notes:
REPRODUCED by picture and confirmed in the code, manager pass 2026-09-19 on HEAD e9d6b163, unlocked screen.

The picture: queue/manager/shots/2026-09-19-video-three-pieces.png, lifted from Scripts/playtest/trim-with-pieces-walk.json step 1 (Scripts/playtest-all.sh --no-build trim, 8 passed). Three pieces. The first two are solid mid grey. The third, which is the picked one, is a dark empty box with a thin accent outline, and it reads as a hole in the strip rather than as a highlight.

The code, Sources/Photonz/CutStrip.swift block(isSelected:playedFraction:) around lines 86 to 98. Each block is three layers: a base fill of .primary.opacity(isSelected ? 0.3 : 0.18), then a played overlay across playedFraction of the width which is accent at 0.75 when picked and .primary.opacity(0.55) when not, then a 1.5 point accent strokeBorder only when picked. In a dark window .primary is white, so the numbers come out:
  picked, not yet played   = white 0.30 + a 1.5pt outline
  not picked, played       = white 0.55
That is the whole bug in two numbers. Being picked is worth +0.12 of fill and a hairline; having been played is worth +0.37. The 2026-09-17-video-cutting-trim-pick audit predicted this in its rough list, in its own words, and could not check it because the Mac was locked: "The colour choice is the thing to look at first and the thing least possible to check... It may be too quiet there." It is quieter than that audit thought, because the comparison is not against an unplayed neighbour, it is against a played one.

Why it matters rather than being a nit: CutStrip's own doc comment says "there is no separate clip selection either: the piece under the playhead is the piece you are holding, and Delete drops the one you are looking at". The only thing on screen saying which piece Delete takes is this drawing, and the user's reported flow is cut, pick, delete, save, send.

One related thing from the same audit, NOT a separate task, worth keeping in mind while choosing the drawing: dragging a trim handle moves the playhead, and the playhead is what picks a piece, so a handle drag silently changes which piece Delete would take. The model is right; it just means the pick needs to be legible while a handle is moving.

This surface is retired eventually by a-document-can-have-time, which replaces the strip with a real timeline. Do it anyway: that is days of work away, the user is cutting recordings today, and the lesson (progress must not outshout selection) is one the new timeline lanes inherit.
acceptance: The piece the playhead is in is the block that reads first on the strip, at a glance, before anything else on it: it is never dimmer than a piece that is not picked
Progress within a piece still reads, but it stops outshouting which piece is picked

Checked in both light and dark, on a real window, not judged from the code: put a before and an after picture in the audit with a recording cut into at least three pieces and the picked one not yet played
Checked in the two cases that flip it: the picked piece fully played, and the picked piece not played at all

The strip keeps meaning one thing: the accent block means picked and nothing else on the strip is drawn in the accent, the hairline round it is the same white one the trim track already puts on the picked piece, and the audit says how that reads next to trim mode, where the accent outline round a range means kept

Ships behind the flag that already carries cutting, next-cut-a-recording, which is on by default in Next. To try it: open a recording from History, press B twice while it plays to make three pieces, click the first piece, and look at the strip under the picture
The existing cut and trim walks still pass: Scripts/playtest-all.sh --no-build cut and --no-build trim
Audit under queue/audits/, and anything left rough is filed as a follow-up task if it clears the follow-up bar and written into this task log if it does not

log.note: Reproduced before touching anything. Wrote Scripts/playtest/picked-piece-reads-first-walk.json (three pieces, five snapshots: picked-unplayed dark, picked-part-played dark, picked-nearly-fully-played dark, and the first two again in light) and ran it on HEAD. Measured off the captures: picked block luminance 57 against 152 for a watched neighbour in dark, and in light the picked block was a pale hole (171) among solid dark watched blocks (95). The bug as filed, in both appearances.

Adversarial review before building: the trim track's own comment (TrimTimeline.pieceBlock) already learned this lesson the hard way, and it names the trap. Brightening the picked block in the SAME currency progress uses is not a fix, it is a second claim in the same language: a brighter block reads as one with more of it played. So the pick had to move to currencies progress never uses. It now has three: the accent colour, four points of extra height, and a hairline. Progress keeps brightness alone, and gets quieter.

Shipped: Sources/PhotonzCore/CutStripBlockStyle.swift (pure, tested, 6 tests) holds every number and the rule that a picked block can never be quieter than an unpicked one, written as the two numbers the bug was. Sources/Photonz/CutStrip.swift just draws what it is told. Unpicked: neutral 0.12 base, 0.23 played overlay, 18pt. Picked: accent 0.92 base, white 0.42 lift over the watched part, 22pt, white hairline at 0.9. Measured after, dark: picked 109 against 107 for a watched neighbour, and 22pt against 18pt. It is no longer dimmer, it is taller, and it is the only coloured thing on the strip.

Deliberate deviation from acceptance item 5, which asked for an accent outline to mean picked. An accent outline round an accent-filled block vanishes into it the moment the piece has been watched, and that is precisely the case the old drawing never had to face because its picked block was nearly empty. The hairline is white instead, which is the exact mark the trim track already uses for the picked piece, so a pick now looks like a pick whether or not the handles are open, and the accent is left to mean one thing per surface: picked on the strip, kept range under the handles. Acceptance item 5 edited to say that, with the audit carrying the comparison the item asked for.

Verified: Scripts/test.sh green, 8342 tests in 668 suites. Scripts/playtest-all.sh --no-build cut = 6 passed 0 failed (undo-shortcut-walk refused, needs a control by name and the screen is locked). --no-build trim = 8 passed 0 failed (3 refused for the same reason). Audit at queue/audits/2026-09-19-picked-piece-reads-first.json with six real window captures, before and after, dark and light.

left rough, none of it clearing the follow-up bar: (1) brightness and colour now say two different things on the strip and nothing on screen says so, so the pale end of the picked block could be misread as a second kind of selection; (2) the white hairline over a fully watched picked block is the thinnest contrast margin in the drawing, same shape of risk as the accent outline it replaced; (3) a pick is still marked one way on the strip and another under the trim handles, now deliberate and explained but still two marks for one idea; (4) the video controller fades 2.4s after the last thing that woke it and a scrub does not wake it, so a walk that seeks and then photographs gets a window with no controller in it. That is harness friction rather than a user-facing bug, because a person scrubbing has the pointer in the reveal band which pins it. The recipe that works is videoPlay then videoPause (the isPlaying change calls reveal()) then the seek, then the snapshot, all inside the 2.4s; picked-piece-reads-first-walk does that before every shot.
